                            ON BEHALF OF AARON EDWARD HOWTON

I, Aaron Edward Howton, submit this Direct Testimony as a pro se intervenor and affected landowner in PUC

59475. I stipulate that this Direct Testimony may be treated by all parties as if the answers were filed under
oath, subject to the verification and affidavit included below. I reserve the right to supplement, correct, or

I. INTRODUCTION, STANDING, AND BACKGROUND
Q. Please state your name and address.

A. My full name is Aaron Edward Howton. My address is 12600 FM 2843, Salado, Texas 76571, Bell County.

Q. Are you an intervenor in this proceeding?

A. Yes. I am a landowner affected by this proceeding. Although I did not receive notice concerning proposed
Link F20 until March 31, 2026, I filed a Request to Intervene through the PUC Interchange on April 18, 2026,
                                                           Page 3

                                                            Page 3
                  Direct Testimony of Aaron Edward Howton I PUC Docket No. 59475 I SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349

referencing PUC Docket No. 59475, Link F20, and Tract 5645. My understanding is that my Request to
Intervene was approved on April 19, 2026. I also filed a Protective Order Certification on April 28,2026.

Q. Are you the owner of Tract 5645 in Bell County?

A. Yes. My wife and I own Tract 5645 in Bell County. The property includes our habitable residence, which is
approximately 142 feet from our property boundary and within 500 feet of the centerline of proposed Route
894, Link F20. See AEH Exhibit 1.

Q. Please summarize your education and professional background.

A. I graduated from Texas A&M; University in 1970 with a Bachelor of Science degree in Wildlife Science.
Following graduation, I served honorably in the United States Air Force from 1971 to 1974, where I worked as
an Engineering Entomologist. From 1974 to 1978, I was employed as an Inspector with the United States
Department of Agriculture, Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service, Plant Protection and Quarantine. In
that role, I was responsible for identifying organisms entering the United States and applying regulatory
inspection and enforcement activities related to agricultural protection. From 1978 to 1982, I served as a
Special Agent, Criminal Investigations, with the USDA Office of Inspector General, where I conducted
criminal investigations involving federal statutory and regulatory violations and enforcement matters. From
1983 until my retirement in 2009, I was employed as Deputy Director of Emergency Services at Fort Hood,
Texas. In that capacity, I had leadership and oversight responsibilities involving federal police, federal game
wardens, military police criminal investigations, fire department operations, physical security, anti-terrorism
programs, and force-protection initiatives. Since retiring from federal service, I have been engaged in church,
livestock farming, and wildlife-management activities on my personal property. See AEH Exhibits 2 and 3.

Q. Will your property be affected by the transmission line project proposed by Oncor Electric Delivery
Company LLC and LCRA Transmission Services Corporation?

A. Yes. The centerline of the proposed 765-kV transmission line on Route 894, Link F20, appears to be
approximately 100 feet from my property boundary and approximately 242 feet from my residence. See AEH
Exhibit 4.



IU. PURPOSE AND NATURE OF TESTUMONY
Q. What is the purpose of your testimony?

A. The purpose of my testimony is to provide information and evidence showing that Route 894, and more
specifically Link F20, is not the most reasonable or prudent routing alternative under the applicable PUC
routing criteria. Link F20 would impose disproportionate and avoidable adverse impacts on my property and
surrounding community, including environmental harm to habitat and wildlife, property devaluation, health
and safety concerns, harm to agricultural and livestock operations, wildfire risk, and disruption to a rural
community still recovering from a Level 3 tornado. I also provide recommendations for alternative routes
because feasible alternatives appear to be available that would substantially reduce the impacts described in
my testimony. My substantive concern is whether prudent avoidance was applied as an affirmative obligation
where my residence is close to the proposed centerline and my property contains habitat associated with
endangered species.

Q. What is the basis of your testimony?



                                                           Page 4

                                                            Page 4
                   Direct Testimony of Aaron Edward Howton I PUC Docket No. 59475 I SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349

A. My testimony is based on my education and training as a wildlife biologist, my personal observations,
firsthand knowledge, and direct experience regarding my property, including its use, infrastructure, water
resources, wildlife habitat, wildfire risk, and planned future residential and agricultural use. To the extent I
offer opinions, those opinions are rationally based on my firsthand knowledge and are offered as lay opinion
testimony. To the extent I reference publicly available studies, agency reports, legislative materials, scientific
literature, or statements by others, I do so to explain the basis of my concerns and understanding of potential
impacts. I am not offering retained expert testimony.

Q. Were you given adequate time to respond to the notice you received?

A. No. I did not receive notice regarding Docket No. 59475 or the proposed Link F20 within 500 feet of my
property until March 31, 2026. The notice advised of an April 27,2026 deadline to intervene and a May 13,
2026 deadline to file direct testimony. My understanding is that some property owners had substantially more
time to respond. I believe the shortened time available to me and similarly situated landowners affected my
ability to fully evaluate and respond to the routing proposal.

Q. Do you believe the Applicants fully accounted for the statutory routing factors?

A. No. Texas Utilities Code Section 37.056 requires consideration of multiple factors, including community
values, recreational and park areas, historical and aesthetic values, environmental integrity, and other impacts.
It appears that the Applicants compared routes using measurements such as mileage, cost, length, paralleling
existing rights-of-way, habitable structures, parks, cropland, rangeland, ripa]ian areas, wetlands, stream
crossings, habitat, cultural sites, airports, highways, and similar measurable factors. However, I do not believe
the routing analysis adequately compares the routes based on community values, historical and aesthetic
values, or the full effects on consumers and landowners. I also understand that some information was derived
from documentation, maps, and flyovers rather than field confirmation. Earlier outreach to affected
landowners would have provided more accurate information for the Commission.



Il DESCROPTOON AND LOCATION OF PROPERTY
Q. Please describe your property and its location.

A. My property is Tract 5645, approximately 46 contiguous acres that my wife and I purchased in 1998. It
consists of fenced farmland and woodland with native and planted grasses and an Ashe-juniper, oak, and elm
mix. The property is located in Bell County, Texas at 12600 FM 2843 near First Cedar Valley Baptist Church.
The property includes our only residence, barns, related outbuildings, farm equipment, and livestock. Our farm
is registered with the USDA Farm Service Agency as Farm ID No. 8538 and with the Texas Comptroller's
Office. See AEH Exhibit 5.

Q. What routes do you oppose?

A. I oppose Route 894 because it includes Link F20. I also oppose any route that uses Link F20 or Link F23.
My understanding is that a large majority of the routes presented by Oncor/LCRA avoid Links F20 and F23,
and that the seven least expensive routes avoid those links. Route 894 does not have the fewest habitable
structures within 500 feet; my understanding is that Route 442 has fewer. Route 894 would traverse a tornado-
damaged community, endangered-species habitat, and an area near a populated church. For those reasons, I do
not believe Route 894 satisfies prudent-avoidance principles when compared to available alternatives.

Q. Do you have photographs or other materials depicting the property?


                                                            Page 5

                                                             Page 5
                   Direct Testimony of Aaron Edward Howton I PUC Docket No. 59475 I SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349

A. Yes. Photographs, aerial images, route maps, and other materials are attached as AEH exhibits.



IV. SUMMARY OF POSUTION AND OMPACTS ON PROPERTY
Q. How is Tract 5645 used today, and how may the proposed transmission line affect that use?

A. Tract 5645 is our home, and we also use it for family recreation, livestock, poultry, agricultural activities,
wildlife habitat, and related rural land uses. A 765-kV transmission line on Link F20 would adversely affect
our home, land, agricultural operations, livestock and pets, recreation, and wildlife habitat. The line would
directly affect habitat for the federally protected Golden-cheeked Warbler, cause significant property
devaluation, raise health and safety concerns related to electromagnetic fields and corona effects, increase
wildfire risk, and potentially disrupt wildlife, pollinators, and livestock operations. See AEH Exhibits 6,7,8,
11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, and 18.


V. COMMUNITY VALUES AND TORNADO RECOVERY
Q. How would the proposed transmission line affect your rural community and community values?

A. Our Cedar Valley community is still recovering from a direct hit by a Level 3 tornado on April 12, 2022.
Most homes have been rebuilt or repaired, and community infrastructure has been restored. First Cedar Valley
Baptist Church has been completely rebuilt. Governor Greg Abbott declared Cedar Valley a disaster area in
April 2022. Four years later, this proposed 765-kV transmission line would place new utility infrastructure in
the same area where residents have spent years cleaning up, rebuilding, and recovering. Proposed Link F20
would concentrate harm on a small number of rural residents, a church, and a central community institution. In
my opinion, that would undermine ongoing disaster recovery and community stability. Selection of Link F20
would be inconsistent with routing principles that should preserve community values and limit landowner
impact where reasonable alternatives exist. See AEH Exhibits 8, 9, and 10.



VO. WILDLIFE, ENDANGERED SPECIES, AND ENVRONMENTAL IMPACTS
Q. What is your most significant wildlife concern if Link F20 is approved as part of Route 894?

A. Although our property supports whitetail deer, wild turkey, fox squirrels, rabbits, foxes, raccoons,
songbirds, and other wildlife, my greatest concern is the Golden-cheeked Warbler. The entirety of our property
lies within an area identified by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service as nesting and breeding habitat for the
Golden-cheeked Warbler, an endangered species protected under the Endangered Species Act. The USDA
Natural Resources Conservation Service identified my property as Golden-cheeked Warbler habitat using the
Six Criteria Identification Guide while surveying my property for the Environmental Quality Incentives
Program. I have personally confirmed those findings using the same NRCS criteria and documented my
findings in writing dated April 5,2026. I have also observed Golden-cheeked Warblers on our property within
500 feet of proposed Link F20. USFWS has identified habitat destruction as the single largest threat to the
GCW. Clearing a 200-foot right-of-way along or near our property boundary may destroy nesting and breeding
habitat, fragment remaining habitat, and reduce species viability. If the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service requires
mitigation, consultation, or an incidental-take process because of habitat impacts, the overall cost and timing
of the project may be affected. Those potential compliance costs should be considered when comparing Link
F20 with routes that do not traverse similar habitat. See AEH Exhibits 11, 12, and 13.

Q. What additional environmental impacts concern you?


                                                            Page 6

                                                             Page 6
                  Direct Testimony of Aaron Edward Howton I PUC Docket No. 59475 I SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349

A. The general area is also associated with the Whooping Crane migration corridor, Monarch butterfly
concerns, and potential habitat for the Salado Salamander. There is also a natural spring lake and Buttermilk
Creek within the broader area near Link F20. I am concerned that routing a 765-kV line through this area will
increase environmental risks, fragment habitat, and impose unnecessary impacts where feasible alternatives are
available. See AEH Exhibit 14.

Q. What risks do you see to birds, pollinators, and native wildlife?

A. Whooping Cranes may be at risk of collision or contact with high-voltage lines because Central Texas lies
within their migration corridor between the Texas Gulf Coast and Canada. Clearing trees for a 200-foot right-
of-way would degrade nesting and foraging habitat used by Golden-cheeked Warblers and migrating Black-
chinned Hummingbirds. Hummingbirds play an important role in pollination, and disruption to their behavior
could impair local plant reproduction and the broader ecosystem. We also have natural Western Honey Bee
hives, which are vital to local ecosystems and agriculture. I am concerned that electromagnetic fields, corona
noise, herbicide maintenance, right-of-way clearing, and construction disturbance could adversely affect
pollinators and other wildlife. I offer these concerns based on my observations, my background, and the
materials identified in the exhibit index, not as retained expert testimony. See AEH Exhibits 7 and 14.



Vl HEALTH, SAFETY, FIRE, AGRICULTURAL, AND PROPERTY-VALUE OMPACTS
Q. What health concerns do you have regarding a 765-kV transmission line near your residence?

A. My residence is approximately 242 feet from the proposed centerline of Link F20. I am concerned about
continuous long-term residential exposure to electromagnetic fields, audible corona discharge noise, and
related stress and sleep disruption. I understand that existing exposure guidelines may address certain
measured thresholds, but I believe the Commission should consider prudent avoidance and the precautionary
principle where habitable structures, a church, and elderly residents are located close to a proposed 765-kV
line. See AEH Exhibit 16.

Q. What do you see as the greatest safety risk from the proposed line?

A. The greatest safety risk is an uncontrolled wildfire in a rural area with habitable structures, limited access,
dry cedar vegetation, and recovering storm-damaged land. I am also concerned about cumulative exposure and
safety effects because there is already an existing Bartlett Electric transmission line along my east property
boundary. See AEH Exhibit 15.

Q. How would the proposed line affect your agricultural activities and animals?

A. My property is an active agricultural operation. We have registered Hereford show cattle and poultry, along
with other agricultural uses. Construction, operation, and maintenance of a high-voltage line in close proximity
to livestock and forage areas may reduce usable grazing land, stress livestock, affect animal behavior, and
introduce herbicide-drift concerns during right-of-way maintenance. See AEH Exhibit 17.

Q. Will proposed Link F20 affect the value and marketability of your property?

A. Yes. Proposed Link F20 would traverse the fulllength of my property's east boundary and would create a
permanent utility corridor next to my home and agricultural improvements. The line would be fully visible
from my residence and would permanently change the property's aesthetics and marketability. I believe the
presence of a 765-kV line, close to the home and associated with environmental, health, safety, and
agricultural concerns, would substantially and permanently reduce the value of the property. A computer-

generated photo of the 765-kV transmission line from my residence balcony is included for review. See AEH
Exhibit 18.

Q. Do you anticipate cumulative impacts?

A. Yes. The proposed Link F20 would be located near an existing Bartlett Electric transmission line along my
east property boundary. Additional clearing, repeated heavy-equipment use, right-of-way maintenance, visual
impacts, and possible cumulative electromagnetic effects would further concentrate harms in the same area
where the community was struck by a Level 3 tornado and is still rebuilding.


Val RECOMMENDATOONS FORALTERNATOVE ROUTES
Q. Can you recommend an alternative route?

A. Yes. Based on the information available to me, Route 767 appears preferable to Route 894. Route 767
appears to better parallel existing linear infrastructure, including transmission corridors, pipelines, or roadway
alignments, for a greater portion of its length. Increased co-location reduces the need to create new corridors
across previously undisturbed properties, limits visual and land-use disruption, and is consistent with the
Commission's preference for paralleling compatible infrastructure where feasible. Route 767 also appears to
offer environmental advantages over Route 894 by reducing impacts to sensitive areas and reducing the direct
burden on the Cedar Valley community and properties affected by Link F20. Although Route 767 may have a
higher estimated cost than Route 894, I understand that cost is not the controlling factor. A modest increase in
cost may be justified where a route materially reduces residential impacts, uses existing corridors, and lowers
environmental and endangered-species risks. For those reasons, I ask the Commission to reject Route 894 and
approve Route 767 or another route that better balances engineering feasibility, cost, landowner impacts,
community values, and environmental integrity. See AEH Exhibit 19.

Q. Are there other routes that appear to have less impact on property owners or sensitive resources?

A. Yes. Several other routes should be studied in detail for community impact. Based on the information
available to me: Route 296 appears to be a close structural match to Route 894 at a relatively modest cost
difference while avoiding Links F20 and F23; Route 442 appears to have fewer habitable structures within 500
feet than Route 894; and Routes 546 and 551 appear to have reduced endangered-species habitat impact and
lower cost in comparison to Route 894. These alternatives further show that Link F20 is not necessary to meet
the project's objectives. See AEH Exhibit 19.


IX. CONCLUSOON AND REQUESTED RELIEF
Q. Please summarize your conclusion.

A. For the reasons stated above, Link F20 is inferior to available alternatives because it would impose
avoidable and disproportionate impacts on my property and community, including confirmed or likely
endangered-species habitat concerns, concentrated harm to a disaster-recovery community, impacts near a
church, wildfire risk, agricultural impacts, property-value impacts, and failure to minimize adverse impacts
under the routing criteria.

Q. What relief do you request?

A. I respectfully request that the Public Utility Commission of Texas and the Administrative Law Judges:

1. Reject Route 894 and any route that uses Link F20 as a viable routing option;

2. Require the Applicants to provide a full Endangered Species Act compliance analysis and presence study
for Route 894 and specifically Link F20;

3. Require the Applicants to pursue ESA Section 10 permitting, if required, and determine whether any federal
nexus exists or is anticipated such that ESA Section 7 consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service is
required;

4. Require a licensed Texas appraiser to assess property-value impacts to Tract 5645;

5. Require an independent third-party electrical or power-engineering consultant to perform on-site modeled
EMF field-strength data collection at Tract 5645 and First Cedar Valley Baptist Church, including peak-load
scenarios at varying distances and six-foot heights; and

6. Reevaluate alternative routes, including Route 767, Route 296, Route 442, Route 546, Route 551 and any
other route that avoids protected habitat, maximizes distance from residences, and minimizes community and
environmental impacts.

Q. Does this conclude your testimony?

A. Yes.

                                         II. ARGUMENT
A. Prefiled Direct Testimony Is Proper Evidence When Sponsored by the Witness.
        SOAH Rule 155.429 expressly allows direct testimony to be filed in writing before the
hearing in narrative or question-and-answer form. Once the wimess is sworn and identifies the
written testimony as a true record of what the wimess would have testified to orally, the written
testimony may be admitted into evidence as if read or presented orally. See 1 Tex. Admin. Code
§ 155.429(c)(1)(A)-(D).
        The PUC's rule governing written testimony is consistent with that procedure. Written
testimony may be received as an exhibit and incorporated into the record without being read
aloud, provided the wimess is sworn, confirms that the testimony is true and accurate, and
submits to cross-examination, clarifying questions, redirect examination, and recross-
examination. See 16 Tex. Admin. Code § 22.225(b).
       For that reason, Mr. Howton's filed Direct Testimony should not be characterized as
inadmissible hearsay merely because it was filed before the hearing. It is the method ordered and
permitted for presenting direct testimony in this case. Mr. Howton will sponsor the testimony
under oath and will be available for cross-examination.
B. Mr. Howton Is Qualified by Knowledge, Skill, Experience, Training, and Education.
